newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bonds close down amid payrolls, Fed jitters.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bonds close down amid payrolls, Fed jitters.

text.p: The U.S. 30-year Treasury bond ended lower on Thursday, reflecting the market's anxiety about the August employment report and its potential implications for U.S. monetary policy.
Treasuries were off to a weak start from the opening as an unexpected 15,000 decline in jobless claims in the week ended August 31 heightened fears of strong payroll creation.
Claims retreated to 316,000, a level economists say is consistent with payroll gains of about 250,000 a month -- not a sign of the slowdown forecast by the Federal Reserve.

A Reuter survey ahead of the August employment report, set for release on Friday at 1230 GMT, puts payrolls at up 244,000 vs. up 193,000 in July, the unemployment rate at 5.3 percent vs. 5.4 percent, and average hourly earnings at up 0.3 percent vs. down 0.2 percent.

"People are nervous as hell. The only longs are the wrong longs, set up by people who bought them at 7.0 percent (bond yield) while trying to anticipate a bottom that did not materialize," said economist Mike Casey at MFR Inc.
"You thought there was value at 7.0 percent and now at 7.15 percent, there isn't any," Casey stressed.

Casey also pointed out the long bond is very vulnerable on the technical charts because there is no major support between the 7.15- and 7.25-percent yield. The bond yield set an intraday high at 7.25 percent on July 8, following a strong June job report.
"It all depends very, very much on the (job) numbers. We can go straight to 7.25 percent," Casey added.

The 6-3/4 percent 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended down 20/32 at 95-01/32 to yield 7.15 percent. At the other end of the curve, the three-month bill discount rate rose four points to 5.22 percent for a yield equivalent of 5.36 percent.
